# Agama on Stellar: the full dossier

Deposit a tokenized stock, get more of it back. Live on Stellar testnet at https://app.agama.finance/stellar-rwa,
code at https://github.com/agamafinance/agama-stellar.

## The problem

A holder of a tokenized share can only hold it. There is no productive use for it on chain: no
yield, no credit, nothing but custody with extra steps. The obvious answer, lend against it, is the
one that takes the share away: a lending market sells the collateral the moment the price falls, and
the share is what the holder came for.

## What Agama does

Two products, both built on the same position.

**Earn.** Deposit a stock and keep it. A share of its value is borrowed against it on Blend at the
level the user picks, and those dollars go to work in a private-credit vault. Permissionless agents
hold that level as the price moves: a rise borrows more into the vault, and a fall is repaid out of
the protocol's own buffer, in the same transaction that notices it, so no stock is ever sold. The
vault yield above the debt is bought back as more of the stock, so what grows is the share count.

**Amplify.** Deposit a stock and hold a multiple of it. The protocol borrows against the deposit,
buys more of the same stock and pledges that too. A multiple of L carries an LTV of (L-1)/L, so the
market's own ceiling caps it at 1/(1-ltv), which is 3.33x at a 70% market. Agents hold the multiple,
buying when it rises and selling only what repays when it falls, with the sale sized to the debt
rather than to the position, so what goes back is the stock the loan bought and never the deposit.

**The buffer is the part of the design that is not free.** The vault does not pay out on demand: a
withdrawal is a request in a FIFO queue, which is the honest behaviour of a credit book, because the
money is lent out. That collides with the one promise the product makes, so the core keeps a USDC
buffer: a fall is repaid from it immediately and a withdrawal request refills it behind the user
rather than in front of them. `buffer()` is public so anyone can see how much is left.

## How it is built

Five Soroban contracts in Rust, 75 tests:

- **core**: the markets, both products, the buffer, and the three agents (rebalance, compound,
  liquidate). The only contract that knows what healthy means.
- **position**: one contract per (owner, market, product). It is Blend's borrower of record, which
  is what keeps one user's trouble off another user's position.
- **oracle**: SEP-40, with RedStone payload parsing and signature verification on chain. Three
  independent signers minimum, a maximum age, and a maximum move per update.
- **vault**: the testnet stand-in for the Agama credit vault, carrying the two properties the
  protocol is built around: a deposit lands immediately, a withdrawal queues.
- **stock**: a SEP-41 stand-in share with a public faucet that mints a fixed quantity on a cooldown,
  because a faucet that takes an amount is a mint function with a friendly name.

Around them: a Python keeper that rebuilds RedStone payloads byte for byte and verifies its own work
by recovering each signer locally before sending; a Next.js app forked from the production front, so
Stellar sits beside the other networks rather than beside a demo; and scripts that deploy, verify and
replay both products end to end on chain.

## What testnet forced, which mainnet would not have

**Our own instance of Blend.** A pool lets nobody borrow until its backstop is funded, a backstop is
funded in BLND:USDC Comet LP, and on testnet neither token is mintable by anyone but its admin.
Blend's shared instance is permanently supply-only for us. So Blend's own contracts are deployed by
us, unmodified: same wasm, same request codes, same interest model. Learning its arithmetic cost
real time: the backstop threshold is balance_blnd^4 * balance_usdc >= 1e25 (our first attempt landed
at 1.99e24), Comet refuses a one-sided deposit above 30% of the balance it holds (ErrMaxInRatio, 17),
and a reserve queued against a pool that is already live is timelocked for a week (InitNotUnlocked,
1203), which froze one pool's asset list around tokens we had already abandoned and cost us the pool.

**A stand-in vault.** The live Agama vault takes Circle's USDC and nobody but Circle mints that.

**Two admin-priced markets.** RedStone carries SPY only as SPY---PRE_AFTER and BENJI as
BENJI_ETHEREUM_FUNDAMENTAL, and the deployed oracle was bound to SPY and BENJI before that was known.

## The walls, and what each one taught

**Soroban's authorization is exactly one frame deep.** A contract authorizes the call it makes
itself and nothing below it, so a pool pulling tokens two frames down fails with
Error(Auth, InvalidAction) and no hint as to which frame. Positions build InvokerContractAuthEntry
trees with authorize_as_current_contract for every pull they are responsible for. The other half of
the same rule: a call a contract must authorize has to be made by that contract, which is why the
positions, not the core, talk to the vault.

**The leveraged product did not fit in a transaction.** Run literally, the Amplify loop exceeds
Soroban's CPU budget and still converges from below: eight passes reach 3.14x of the 3.33x on offer,
in sixteen calls into the pool. It is settled in one step instead: advance the whole multiple, pledge
it, borrow against the full position and keep the dollars as payment. Identical to the loop's limit,
exactly rather than approximately, in two pool calls.

**Health is checked per request, not per transaction.** Tests green, chain answering InvalidHf
(1205): Blend evaluates each request in a submit as it applies it. Pledge before borrowing, repay
before withdrawing. The mock that let it pass checked nothing, which is the real lesson: a mock that
cannot refuse proves nothing about a chain that can.

**A passkey account cannot sign a call into your contract.** Nido smart accounts are in the wallet
picker. A Perch account's passkey signs only under its own admin rule, scoped to the account itself,
so a call into the protocol comes back #3014 or #3002, by design. Acting for one means session keys:
the owner approves a Perch rule naming a key the app holds as a delegated signer on one contract, for
one list of functions, under a cap only a transfer can carry (#3223 otherwise, and an uncapped rule
allows no token function at all). One rule per contract in the call's authorization tree.

**A wallet forced a protocol change.** The one-click faucet made a single signature cover eleven
token faucets, each checking it on the way down. For a passkey account that is twelve confirmations
before anything arrives, so the core now mints the drip itself and asks nobody to authorize anything.

**And a bug only a passkey found.** Closing a position the minute it was opened was impossible: the
close repays from the buffer and files the refund against the position's vault balance, but a debt
grows in Blend's d_rate by the second while a vault share price does not follow it. The vault refused
to burn shares that were not there (#3), 213 stroops short on the position that found it. The request
is now for what the position holds and the buffer carries the difference.

**RedStone closed its public gateways mid-build.** 403 inside windows that grow every day, nothing at
all from 29 October 2026. The keeper takes an authenticated gateway through configuration now, and
when it has none it says what happened and what to do.

## Signing for a passkey account, in practice

Every action renews the rule it needs with the passkey and runs under it a second later: one
confirmation per action, which is what a signature per action means for an account of this kind. The
alternative, approving once and then acting silently for a day, is the same rules with nobody
watching them being used. The ceremony is a page navigation, so the action is armed in localStorage
and run on the way back, once, and the page comes back where it was left.

Verified end to end against the real network and the real Nido, with a Chrome virtual authenticator
answering the passkey: an account made, connected, funded, granted, a deposit of 5 TSLAx at 56% LTV,
a close that hands all ten back, an Amplify that holds 14.9 TSLAx on a deposit of 5, and an unwind.
Five ceremonies, five calls, five minutes, no fingerprint. `node scripts/nido/e2e.mjs`.

## Verifying any of this

    ./scripts/verify.sh            everything, in one pass, 19 checks
    cargo test                     the contracts, 75 tests
    ./scripts/e2e.sh               an Earn, start to finish, on chain
    ./scripts/amplify-e2e.sh       an Amplify, the same
    node scripts/nido/e2e.mjs      the same, for a passkey smart account
    python3 keeper/run.py once     relay prices, then let the agents act

    oracle   CBTNXB4KM4UKW25Z6UF22FOABSYS6AFJP34Y4DXBCLIQNYVPK255PJ6M
    vault    CCVVFPL5ZUTBEKJYS4AGRPFHLOO42TPTUMACHXBQPUW3YTZ23AIAE5GF
    pool     CCNJ6D3ITLT22QCVNTD3AVEY4ANE3FYXSKIQTLFXTLPOSPWLWWTPHCCG
    USDC     CD5IKHINGOCVAOZPWD4R5R7FVAAZBCZOVQJVGIGI7XMYESK3CVGUVDSL
    TSLAx    CAH4TV2YO3SQ4KEVEQEUKFDDHHDCVDWBGLBGXFF6C5ZPYF7HH5GXVE4Y

Ten markets: TSLAx, NVDAx, AAPLx, MSFTx, AMZNx, GOOGLx, METAx, SPYx, BENJI and GOLDx. Every one
carries the same 7000 bps of LTV, and that is the design rather than a shortcut: what backs the loan
is not the share's calm, it is the position's own counterweight, and that is the same on Tesla as on
a money fund. What is left of the share's volatility is the part the agents cannot outrun, the gap
when the session is shut, which is what the off-hours buffer is for.
